utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is July 2nd, 2009, and I welcome Mr. Praljak. I greet Mr. Stojic, Pusic, and Petkovic. I welcome everyone from the Defence, as well as everyone from Prosecution, and I greet everyone helping us in this courtroom. Let me first issue an oral decision. It's quite long, and I will read it slowly, because I want it to be well-understood by everyone. Oral decision on the request by the Petkovic Defence to obtain clarifications on time allocation. During the hearing of July 1st, 2009, the Petkovic Defence addressed the Trial Chamber to ask for clarifications regarding the position of the Trial Chamber on the right Defence teams can have to use their own time allocated to present their case in order to cross-examine witnesses. The Trial Chamber reminds the Petkovic Defence of the decisions issued on December 11, 2008, January 12 and 19, 2009, mentioned by the Petkovic Defence, and notably the decision issued on January 19, 2009. In this latter decision, the Trial Chamber first indicated that it had regularly allowed the Defence teams to use their own time allocated to present their case to have additional time used to cross-examine witnesses called by other accused. However, the Trial Chamber added that regarding the specific request, the request for additional time made by the Petkovic Defence was obviously excessive because it greatly changed the hearing schedule of the Stojic Defence and meant, in fact, that the cross-examination of the expert witness would be extended in a way that would be contrary to a fair and expeditious trial. Consequently, when issuing the decisions mentioned above, it was clear that the Trial Chamber was issuing a decision on the request made by the Petkovic Defence in the framework of the cross-examination of the expert witness, Davor Marijan, and only this witness; and that it would not mean that it would ban using the Defence's own time to allocate additional time to cross-examine a witness called by another accused. The Trial Chamber insists on the fact that when it issues decisions regarding time allocation, it is using its discretionary power and its duty to control how a witness is examined in order to make sure that all accused have a fast and fair trial. The Trial Chamber, therefore, challenges any interpretation according to which because a Defence team is asking to use its own time to cross-examine a witness, the Trial Chamber should automatically grant this request. The Trial Chamber recalls that it could only grant such a request if such a request was reasonable and fully grounded. So this is a very long decision, but in a nutshell let me sum it up: In the previous case regarding the expert, the Trial Chamber had decided that providing additional time would change the hearing in an excessive fashion and decided, therefore, not to grant this request, but the decisions will be made on an ad hoc basis. Sometimes it will be possible, and sometimes it won't. The Trial Chamber has a duty to control the examination of witnesses, to make sure that the trial is expeditious. Mrs. Alaburic, this is why the Trial Chamber decided that in the present case with Mr. Praljak you -- if you had wanted additional time, the Trial Chamber saw no problem with it, but they told you that it would be deducted from your own time. As you see, this is fully in line with what had been decided previously, which is why we issued this decision in order to make things crystal clear. Now you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, Your Honours and everybody else in the courtroom. I'm going to say just two sentences by way of explanation for your decision, and I thank you for the prompt decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Just a minute. Mr. Registrar, my headsets aren't working once, unfortunately, once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, all I wanted to say is that the Petkovic Defence is wholly aware of the contents of the decision of the Honourable Trial Chamber of the date mentioned by you, and it is our position -- our position is based on the following parts of that decision: First of all, the observation that our request for using our own time is in complete contradiction with the rules established on the 24th of April, 2008, and that that request, and this is my second point, is contrary to the rights of the accused to an expeditious trial, and those two points are recorded on pages 35157 of the transcript. And as far as my third argument, that is to say that it disrupts the schedule for examination of witnesses, which was the criterion that you mentioned now in your decision, we consider that to the same extent one should respect the schedule of the witness made up by the Praljak Defence team. However, the Petkovic Defence will review your decision, and in conformity with that, we shall decide whether we're going to seek any clarification, challenge it, or whether we're going to take notes of it and continue. So thank you for that. I cannot give you a definite answer at this point in time. Now, with your permission, may I continue my cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can continue later, but personally I'd like to know something. I'd like to get a confirmation, if possible. I'd like to know whether Mr. Petkovic will actually testify, yes or no. If Mr. Petkovic will testify, I will prepare for this testimony. It's a lot of work. It's already a few months before Mr. Praljak testified I had prepared myself. Mr. Praljak will probably finish his testimony during the month of September, and of course I want to get ready for any questions regarding Mr. Petkovic, so I'd like to know whether he will testify or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I can tell you is how our plans stand now. According to our plans, General Petkovic will, indeed, testify, and he will testify at the end of his Defence case, because we, first of all, want to present in full our theory about this whole case; and then finally we would like to give you the opportunity to question General Petkovic about all the theses that we're going to put forward and all the documents that we consider to be relevant, and all the most contentious documents, which are linked to General Petkovic, which my learned friends of the Prosecution mention in their pre-trial brief, as well as all other documents, which in our opinion are most incriminatory for General Petkovic, we are going to consider them part of our direct examination; and we're going to question and examine General Petkovic about that. And I'm sure you will become involved in the discussion of these documents and that we will provide Judge Antonetti with a chance to ask additional questions, and you will of course have the chance of asking any questions you like, and General Petkovic will be happy to answer them all. So those are our plans as they stand for the moment. I think that they will stay that way, and I hope that General Petkovic's health will be as good as it is now and that we'll be able to present all the theses and points that we consider to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'd like to -- well, let me say good morning to you, first of all.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to deal with effective control as efficaciously as possible and look at the 11th element of the 15 that I mentioned that I was going to discuss, and you spoke at length in this courtroom about that. And it is the topic of failure to respond to the mobilisation call and of people voluntarily leaving their units, so let us look at a document that I consider to be highly relevant when discussing that topic. It is still in the first binder, and it is in the fourth group of documents under the title of "Effective control." The document number is 4D1655. As I said, 4D1655 is the document number. And it is an order from the defence minister, Bruno Stojic, dated the 11th of October, 1993. The document is titled a "Order," bit, in fact, it is information, and Mr. Bruno Stojic, in fact, tells the military district prosecutor's office and district military courts and the military police administration of the conclusions made by the parliament of the HR HB and the conclusions of the extended government session, expanded government session. And in those conclusions, he highlights this problem. So let us look at point 1 of that order where it says is that: "All district military courts and district military prosecutor's offices shall give priority for the cases related to the failure to respond to the call for general mobilisation and wilful abandonment of military units." At that time, General Praljak, you were the number one man in the Main Staff, so tell us now, please, in your opinion does this document confirm how these two problems that I've just mentioned were discussed by the top-most bodies of government of the CRHB and they considered them to be important problems for the functioning of the army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the situation: Unless that problem could be solved, the problem -- the army would have been harmed to such an extent that it would have disintegrated and we would have lost territory. We would have been defeated, and then -- well, those courts should work normally looking for criminals, the perpetrators of crimes, and they wouldn't be able to carry on with their daily business. If you lose the war, you can't carry on with your normal business, because five years on, ten years on, you would have to find the criminals and perpetrators, so this is a priority issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I have not prepared document for you on this topic and I'm sorry about that now, although I used it in cross-examining the Prosecutor's witnesses, but there were calls from certain units sent to higher commands. Let's leave aside the prosecution of criminals after combat operation, because if, at this point in time, we have the fate of our municipality in question, then we don't have time to prosecute criminals. That's what they said. And we'll do that next month once we've finished all the military operations. Did you ever come across thoughts and observations and requests of that kind coming in to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mrs. Alaburic, well, there were fewer and fewer people. People were leaving, and then the people who remained asked you, Well, for how long are we going to stay here? Why us? Why only us? And how will those who were considered as traitors, because of being deserters, how were they going to be prosecuted and punished? So this is a logical question. Why did you escape? You escaped and I stayed on. I remained. So how is he going to be sanctioned and punished, while I'm going to be killed; whereas you're swimming along the Adriatic coast or you're in Zagreb or you're in Munich or wherever; so that was a terrible problem. It was a crucial point. And this impaired the morale of the army and their combat readiness to such an extent that their very existence was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General, thank you for that answer. Let's move on to the next portion which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I have a question or two questions. I would be interested to know whether this order had any actual effect and whether it proved -- whether it achieved its goal, and I remember vividly Mr. Praljak telling us that it made no sense to put people into prison, and this does not go very well together with what you have just now said, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, prosecution -- it's like this: People ask for the impossible, and a lot of this just could not be implemented. People came to me and said, General, we don't want to go to the battlefront. We want to go to Makarska - Makarska is Croatia - to round up all those traitors because they said we're not going to the battle-field until we round up all those deserters who are sunning themselves and swimming in Makarska. And it wasn't possible legally for Croatia to round up these deserters. It just wasn't possible. It was sufficient for any of these people to report to an international organisation and say they didn't want to fight a war, and they would be given amnesty automatically. Then there was a proposal to enact a law to seize their property, confiscate their property, but that wasn't possible legally either. And then what happened was that people would set fire to these people's houses during the night. If you just arrest him and put him in prison, then you achieve nothing once again, and among other things, I asked those who be arrested be sent to the front line because the main thing was to have them fight, not to lie in prison doing nothing; so it was difficult to implement all this. Many of those people were no longer on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They had already left. Those who remained and did not respond to the call-up, it was difficult to find them because they would sleep away from home. And if you were able to round up someone, you would have to send them to prison, and it was better for them to be in prison rather than to be out in the cold in the wind and rain. So that's an answer to your question, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, I have a question. Mr. Praljak, what you're explaining is quite honourable. You're talking about this theory of generalised chaos. I'm trying to understand your theory on generalised chaos, but I'm having a difficult time understanding how you justify the fact that military courts were not effective. If I've understood you correctly, you said that there were no sanctions at the time, because for you the sanction would be to put failing soldiers or deserters in gaol, but after all, for them it was better to be in gaol than to be fighting. So this problem of sanctions for militaries during wartime is something that has been extensively studied in military law. It's true that any sanction for armed people, people with weapons, must be immediate. It must inspire fear in order to make sure that the military structure operates properly. If you tell us that the sanctions provided for in your military code book inspired no fear whatsoever, then all I can infer is that your prevailing law at the time had not provided for any sanction. If no sanction had been provided for, it means that there was no law, because the law could only exist if you had sanction; otherwise it's morality, religion, common sense, politeness, diplomacy, whatever, but it's not law. So wasn't there a way to envisage any kind of sanction that would be a good deterrent? I don't know what the situation was like on the field, but it all depends on different armies, they all have their solutions. I can mention a few. I know some military criminal codes where the delinquent can be sent to the front. Those who have been convicted and sentenced, they are actually sent to the first line to fight. I know other military criminal codes where it's just a firing squad, you know, that is provided for for anyone that wants to desert. So how can you say that the military were volunteers and that they -- and that they're not submitted to sanctions? The community is giving you weapons, and because of that, you're placed in a very specific position. Otherwise, you might as well go to the beach, you know, rather than bear weapons to defend a community. So what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can confirm everything you've said. You're quite right. However, as far as I know in military jurisdiction of the HZ HB, that was not how it was. So with respect to the quantity of people violating the law, the courts were impotent. You couldn't execute them, that's for sure. They were, first of all, punished. It's not true that they weren't sanctioned and punished. But I was of the opinion that a term in prison, of course for crimes of murder and so on, there was so much theft as you were able to see, there were so many criminal reports filed, you can see the number, and then you can see how many were convicted, how many were convicted in courts. Counsel for Mr. Coric will be talking about things -- those things. But as far as desertion is concerned, in many countries, it's either a term of -- in prison of 20 to 30 years or execution or the person is sent to the front. Unfortunately, as far as I know, here the sanctions could be, let's say, three months in prison or something like that, which is not really punishment. It's a reward to the person. So it was difficult to uncover the culprits. When you did find them, the imposed sentence could be what -- as I've said, and the soldiers propose that their property be seized. Our lawyers said that that's just not possible, that the two have nothing to do with each other. It's apples and pears. So there was no adequate sanction because the number of these deserters was too great.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Praljak, let's try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, let's try and explain something to Their Honours, because it seems that there's a lack of understanding here. Let's take it this way: Could a soldier go to prison, go into prison, because he was being disciplined by his commander or the military court in question, and the alternative could be that he could be put in prison because he was proclaimed responsible for a crime -- for having committed a crime and then be sent to prison on the basis of a court judgement and sentence? These are two quite different situations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, they are two different situations. The commander could punish him for a term in prison for up to 30 days, as far as I know, and that was it. And we didn't have these courts down there to mete out these sentences. There were no disciplinary courts of that nature. There were no judges or staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, in -- while you were examined so far, you said that it wasn't effective to punish people by sending them to prison because that would be tantamount to a reward compared to those who were sent to the front and had to fight and might be killed. I thought you were thinking about disciplinary measures and punishment taken to -- by the commanders without going into the question of military jurisdiction and jurisprudence and so on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I had the problem when faced with a situation of this kind -- well, of course we did discipline and sanction and use the -- meted out the punishment that we could. But you would always think, now, for a month, he's not going to go to the front. So, in fact, by sending him to prison you've -- well, what I wanted to do was to hand him over to his commander and tell the commander, Send him to the front and watch him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, your answer was not wholly recorded in the transcript, so I will repeat the part of the question, so be so kind as to repeat a part of your answer. You have been talking about disciplinary measures, disciplinary punishment. You did not go into the subject of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had nothing to do with the military judiciary. The moment some proceedings started in any way, we had nothing to do with it, except maybe perhaps for some statements to contribute to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," General Praljak, are you referring to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I hope that we have clarified this segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, another -- there's another aspect to this problem. You said that it was difficult to draft a soldier somewhere in Croatia. Others were swimming in Makarska. I was listening to you, and I wondered whether the problem was even more complicated than that. When you were talking about your own case, said that you were a dual national. You're both -- you have both Croatian nationality as well as nationality from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So a person that lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina but who is of Croatian ethnicity and who holds a Croatian passport and who is in Makarska can say that he's a Croatian citizen, that he has no business in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; but then, in that case, the Republic of Croatia can draft this person as a Croatian citizen if he doesn't do his national service in the forces of the Croatian army, then he could be considered as being a deserter. But if the Republic of Croatia does not draft this person and just tells him, We need you, just volunteer, and he doesn't want to volunteer, then what is the resort left to -- what can the Croatian government resort to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I thought. It can't do anything. It can, however, force a person to go there. In that case, the Republic of Croatia comes up against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. And huge numbers had dual nationalities. And, Your Honours, as far as I know, nothing could be done about that, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify, when the same requests were -- when the same applications were made from Croatia by the government in Sarajevo [as interpreted] for Muslims to be mobilised, and where such requests were made, they would just report to the Red Cross or the organisation, Amnesty International, and there you have it. There was nothing that one could legally do to make them go to war. So the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina also sent the same request to the government of Croatia for its citizens who had fled to be arrested and returned, but as far as I know, that was impossible to do, and it was never done, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something wrong with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Vesna. Thank you. Mr. Praljak's response, page 14, line 20. The General did not say it was a request from the Republic of Croatia to Sarajevo but vice versa, that it was a request made to the Republic of Croatia. So can that be rectified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina also had a huge number of lads who had fled who were fit for service and should have served, and it asked the Croatian government the same thing that the HVO requested but without any success, to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in future I shall keep my eyes more on the transcript, General Praljak, than on you. Let's move on to the topic of the Main Staff with -- with all its aspects, including the role of the Main Staff in the Defence Department, i.e., the Ministry of Defence. Let us initially first clarify a number of elements, General Praljak. You told us that you have not read the indictment, but I will ask you anyway whether you are familiar with the fact that the indictment does not contain charges for crimes of attacks on undefended towns and cities and villages, which is a crime from Article 3, paragraph (C) of the Statute. Are you aware of the fact that such charges do not exist in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I have not read the indictment throughout. I didn't say that I did not read any part of it. I just stopped at a certain count. I just was not able to read on. It is not that I did not try hard to read it. It is just that I didn't. After a certain point, I failed to understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Actually, General, I was trying to say that there are no charges to the effect that there were some activities organised in military terms that could be justified by legitimate military reasons. There are some other crimes which are similar to it, but this is not disputable. Let us now move on to a document, the first in this set of documents of Main Staff. It is 4D1330. This is an interview of the then president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, published in Croatian soldier in April 1992, "Hrvatski Vojnik." General, in the examination-in-chief, you have already presented this interview to us, but a part of the interview which you presented to us was not translated into the English language. That is why I should like you to see this interview now with full translation, and we shall repeat the portion which you read in the direct examination which will be the foundation for our further elaboration. Please look at page 13 of the "Hrvatski Vojnik." In the English version it will be the page marked 4D260978, 0978, and there will be a portion on the following page. General Praljak, I'm going to read it now; namely, President Tudjman says, and I quote: "We received the officer corps of the former JNA on the basis of general programme on the basis of which we are creating the Croatian army, because we knew that 90 per cent of the population of Croatia wanted to participate consciously in the setting up of a Croatian state in all areas, including the military one." Now I'll skip over a part and I'll go on: "Yes, we needed professionals so that we would be able to handle weapons, but we could not just abandon the armed might to cold professionalism. It must be two of that kind of policy that has led to Croatia's independence and that aspires to build Croatia." I shall now again skip a part, and I should like to stress the following: The army's one of the essential elements of state policy, of state independence, and autonomy, and it has to be responsible to that state policy which the people by way of elections -- by way of elections give a vote of confidence to pursue precisely such a state policy, and also I'm skipping another sentence and will go on: "The Main Staff is just a part of the Ministry of Defence for operations and training just like, for example, the IPD information and propaganda service, the military police, the counter-intelligence service, et cetera, exist. They are all component parts of the ministry as a whole. The army cannot only be placed on the professional soldiers. In a democratic system such as we are today building in Croatia, it is the minister of defence who is accountable for the forming of the armed forces on the whole to the government, to the assembly, and to the president of the republic." General Praljak, do you remember that it was precisely these parts that you read out to us when you were examined-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us then, if I remember correctly, that the system was identical -- an identical system as in Croatia was also established in Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you also told us then that it was precisely on the basis of this quotation that within the framework of the Ministry of Defence or the Defence Department there existed parallel services, a Main Staff, an IPD, a SIS service, the military police, the health department, et cetera. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. These are all services which serve in a complicated structure such as the army is for that complicated structure to be able to discharge its duty well. Of course, unfortunately, that requires time and resources and wisdom, et cetera, but the worse the situation is, the worse that functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next document now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment: Will speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This already has a status of an exhibit. It is 42 -- 412 -- 4D1280, 4D1280. Now we have the good number. So look at this diagram. It was made strictly in keeping with the decree on the armed forces. Take a look at the structure of the Defence Department. Does this structure correspond to what your knowledge is of the organisational structure of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. This is the composition of it. This is that diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just some clarification regarding logistics in order to avoid any confusion. Logistics within this structure is when the supply, procurement, and production department, which was one sector within the Defence Department; is that not right, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that exactly. I can't say, frankly speaking. There was a part which was in charge of the production of weapons. There was a section which was in charge of distribution, the main logistical centre, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you. In that connection, do you know that the main logistical base until May 1993 was linked to the Main Staff and that formally -- that is formally, and that later it was also formally incorporated into the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. General, we shall try to deal with the de facto and de jure relationships in the Defence Department. But what we shall try to demonstrate to the -- Their Honours will not be a series of individual decisions. What we wish to show is what was supposed to be done by whom and what was, indeed, done by persons on the basis of plan -- work plans and work reports. Tell me, General, you never worked as a civil servant, but do you, perhaps, know that from the work plans and reports within a state, one can best see what people did and what was in the respective ambits of competence of different individuals; is that logical?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is logical. Whoever appoints someone will be his superior. And, of course, it can be seen by who reports to whom, who is subordinated to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic showed you yesterday a series of documents about how the commanders of individual military units issued orders to their assistants for IPD or for some other sector. I will advance to you the thesis of General Petkovic's Defence, and please tell me whether you agree, General Praljak, namely that the horizontal line between the commanders of a military unit and his assistants [Realtime transcript read in error "assistance"] is something which is not contentious at all and that the commander had a right and obligation to issue orders to his assistants for duties which they were under the obligation to perform.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now try on the basis of the summing up of His Honour Judge Trechsel, who recapitulated in a couple of words the essence of the problem that we have been discussing at some length in this courtroom, to see where the top is of the SIS, of the IDP, of the health department, and of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel could I request a clarification for the transcript? I'm looking at line 10 on page 20. Reference to the horizontal line between the commanders of military unit and his assistants, and I think the word -- I think the intended word is assistants, assistant in the plural, rather than assistance. It's a little bit of nuance of the language, but I think it's an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment, it was assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colleague Stringer. You are quite correct. I was talking about the commander and his assistants, assistants to the commander, his closest associates who were in charge of the different duties, different sectors. Thank you very much, Colleague Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are with the sentence, what, Ms. Alaburic, did you mean when you say "horizontal"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can just complete this segment, we shall be reverting to the organisational schemes of the Defence Department and its individual parts, and we will be dealing with the horizontal and vertical lines of communication. A horizontal line of communication will be the line within a military unit, and a vertical line will be that which goes towards a superior military channel, and we shall see where it ends at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's try to answer a question or, rather, the way Judge Trechsel summed the problem up. I'm very grateful to Judge Trechsel for having done that. And, General Praljak, at your time was the head of the SIS Ivo Lucic or was it you, the commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the SIS and the responsible -- everything that was supposed to be done by the SIS was Mr. Ivo Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, the commander of the military medical services, I would kindly ask the interpreter not to interpret this word as commander. Let us interpret that as the number one man, because that was, indeed, the number one man for medical services. I agree with the number one man or the head of. We're talking about the number one man of the military medical services. Was the number one man of the medical services Dr. Bagaric or you, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now what about the number one man of the IPD sector or the IPD service? Was it Mr. Veso Vegar or you, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Veso Vegar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the head of the military police? Was it Mr. Valentin Coric or you, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the military police -- or, rather, if one unit of the military police was resubordinated to you, General Praljak, as the commander of the HVO, were you responsible for that resubordinated unit of the military police? Go on, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as its operative use went, yes, I was in charge of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at a diagram which will help us clarify the horizontal and vertical lines. The diagrams are in the fourth small binder that we subsequently added to our lot. This is what it looks like. So actually it is not in the binder itself, and the first diagram that I would like to show you is the diagram for the SIS. 4D1281 is the document number. General Praljak, I hope you found the diagram. We've already seen it in this courtroom. Tell us, please, whether this diagram corresponds to what you know about the organisation of the SIS at the time when you were the HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we now try and clarify for the benefit of Their Honours what horizontal lines were, let's start with the operation zone. Would a horizontal line there be the connection between the assistant commander for security with his commander of the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now let's look at the following document. This is the IPD diagram. 4D1284 is the document number. General Praljak, does this diagram correspond what -- to what you know about the organisation of the IPD service at the time when you were the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the diagram representing the medical service. This is 4D1285. Does this diagram correspond to what you know about the organisation of the wartime medical service at the time when you were the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now that we have touched upon the issue of health service, I would like to ask you something as I believe that you still owe an answer to His Honour Judge Trechsel to his very logical observation which was about the detention centre in Prozor, and the observation went as follows: How come that a military commander sent his own doctor to the detention centre and you are saying here, General Praljak, that that commander was not responsible for that detention centre? And I believe that Judge Trechsel's remark was completely founded when he did not see any logic there. Can we try and clarify this lack of logic based on the example of Heliodrom? Tell me, please, whether you know that Heliodrom was a military prison.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Heliodrom was not under the control of any of the military units of the HVO or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that the 3rd Brigade of the HVO was billeted at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on account of the fact that the 3rd Brigade of the HVO was billeted at Heliodrom, it provided logistical support to the military police in that Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no obstacle to that being done since there always problems with logistical support and they had their own mess, their own kitchen. One could issue an order for them to logistically support a prison of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom, Dr. Bagaric told us that the Medical Corps of the 3rd Brigade provided health care services to the military prison, and there are documents to that effect. Do you know that a military brigade, which was billeted in a certain area, provided support to detention centre in any terms, in any way necessary, and in any way requested; and does that make any sense at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but it does make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the following diagram, which is a diagram representing functional links. 4D1286. Look at the diagram, please. The diagram has not been admitted into evidence. Each of the organisational elements of the Defence Department had a certain direct independent link with the armed forces of the HZ HB. When functional links are presented in this way, would they reflect what you know about the situation as it was on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had links. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about parallel chains of command --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to my learned friend for interrupting. Maybe she should explain the diagram. I'm confused by the line that leads from the administration of the military police via the armed forces. Should we completely ignore the armed forces as if they did not exist? It seems that the military police in commander of the armed forces -- I must admit I'm not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will gladly do that, and I apologise to my learned friend for not having spotted that and having not done that, although I knew that this may be a cause for confusion. It's very important to see where the line stops. The line stops with the military police, which under Article 137 of the Decree on Armed Forces is an integral component of the armed forces. In other words, the diagram shows that the administration of the military police had direct links with the military police, but I believe that it would have been much simpler to show it in this way than to draw lines on the side. In other words, this diagram does not -- I apologise. Let me just finish my sentence. This diagram does not say that the administration of the military police had anything whatever to do with the HVO or the armed forces of the HVO or, rather, its military units as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I apologise for rising to interrupt my learned friend. The reason I do so is my learned friend has trespassed, in my respectful submission, into the area of testimony. Of course it's open to any party to seek to admit an exhibit, but the explanation of that must come through a witness, rather than through counsel; and, Your Honour, I think what my learned friend did, just now, was to give evidence, and that is completely inappropriate for counsel to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was responding to a call for explanation by the -- the counsel for Mr. Coric. I believe that her intervention was well in place, and I was also of the opinion that I needed some -- to explain this for the Trial Chamber in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Go on General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and clarify. I was the assistant minister for IPD in the Croatian army. I had my own chief who was my subordinate, a sort of assistant and a deputy, if you will. And it all went down the line, down to the company level. I appointed all of the men irrespective of where proposals came from. There were different proposals. My service did the screening and vetting. We would sometimes ask for the people to be vetted either by the SIS or the civilian police, if there were indications showing that the person in question was not up to the task. A lot of people were new and unknown to us, but it was me, at the end of the day, or my chief who signed the document on their appointment. My remit was to organise seminars on the topic of the international law. I made sure that there was a military orchestra and that it was ready to play, that there were psychologists and that they be employed -- deployed all over the area to talk to people. I was also in charge of the projects showing the situation in the brigade or in the company. I was the one who had to make sure that people trusted their commanders, that they were satisfied with the food, the orders issued to them. I also needed to find out what the causes of crimes were. I maintained contacts with journalists. I was in charge of the editing and publication of "Hrvatski Vojnik." I was the one who was in charge of explanation the scope of the state and military policies. Whatever was needed in the military, I was the one who organised all that. I received reports. I appointed people. Sometimes I would ask for some brigade commanders to be removed, and with that, I would explain that I had received information that that person was not good, that he was doing things that he should not have been doing. So I'm talking about the vertical structure. I was the organiser. I provided support to a huge department which had dozens of duties. And now, on to a brigade commander or the commander of some other unit. Every such person could approach my man and ask him to help him carry out his duties, the duties that he had. If there was a field mission, he could ask him to join him in a field mission. This was the logical organisation of any well-organised army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise I was waiting for Mr. Praljak to finish, but I would like to object to a question. On line 25 -- or, rather, on page 25, line 14, my learned friend started this sentence, which she never finished. But she started it in the following way, "When you were talking about the parallel line of command." I just want to remark for the transcript that on several occasions, Mr. Praljak, in this courtroom, when he was talking about the SIS, the health service, and the IPD, he was talking of the parallel control bodies. He never mentioned, as far as I know, a parallel line of command. Maybe I'm not right. Maybe Mr. Praljak wants to change his position. I don't -- I won't object to that. I would like to state that he never used the word "parallel line of command."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, in that sense, you are right. If we use the word parallel, that would mean existence at the same level, and here we are not talking about parallel but cross-lined. It is true that the brigade commander did have the right to issue orders to the services.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, hold on. Hold on, please. I don't want to waste any time on Mrs. Nozica's objections. Nevertheless, I need to tell you this or ask you this: Have you not been telling us that the SIS, the military police, the IDP were established as parallel systems to exert political control over the military? Isn't that what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did exist in parallel. They were parallel systems. The IPD was, indeed, a parallel system which had its major tasks, which he was or was not able to carry out. On the one hand, we had what was supposed to be done; and on the other hand, we had those things that were, indeed, done. But the IPD was in service of the army to help it be better.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you something that still begs clarification, and it is still a controversial issue. When you were talking about communication between Bagaric, the number one man of the health care service, and Zeljko Siljeg, a commander of the operation zone, you said that Zeljko Siljeg was right and that Dr. Bagaric did not have the -- the authority to issue any orders to military commanders; is that right, General? Let me -- let me guide you through my question. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. He did not have the authority to issue military orders to military commanders, but he did have the right to issue orders to his doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. There was another case that you mentioned, a communication between Veso Vegar and the assistant of a military unit, an assistant for IPD in that military unit, and you told us that Veso Vegar had the authority to issue orders to the assistant commander for IPD; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's summarise. The number one man of the SIS, the number one man of the health care service, the number one man of the IDP did not have the authority to issue orders to military commanders. However, they did have the authority to issue orders to the assistants of the same military commanders for the respective services; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. Let's just clarify the part when you were talking about what you did in the IPD service. I'm talking about your position as the assistant minister of the Republic of Croatia for the IDP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now let's look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I would still like to -- to ask a question about the relationship between military commander and assistant. Another name for the assistant would be chief of service, of the medical service, of information service, and so forth. Is it not one of the tasks of these specialists, medical, and so forth, to advise the commander. When the commander makes an order for an operation, a bigger order, then in that order are conclude -- included not only the operative ones, the 1st Battalion goes there, the 2nd there, and so forth, but also orders pertaining to the medical service, to logistics, and so forth? And is not one of the main tasks of the assistants to advise the commander so that the commander has the command authority, but the substance is delivered or proposed by the assistants?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, you're quite right. Precisely that. If you want an explanation, I can tell you what that looks like when you're sitting down at a table planning something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I have written many such orders in my life, so I have an experience. Without wishing to pose as an expert, of course, but in my country for -- for a large amount of the citizens, it is an experience that they have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we understand what you are saying when there is a parallel chain to control the commander of the brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're saying. I understand there's a necessity for control, but, on the other hand, militarily-wise, I really am in the dark. Let me give you an example. Let's assume that a brigade commander is going to conduct a military operation, so he brings together all his assistants, all these officers in order to prepare for the operation, and he says, Tomorrow at 6.00, we will attack the enemy, at 6.00 a.m. There will probably be casualties, fatalities, so civilian protection must be able to do its job and pick up the corpses. So the assistant in charge of civilian protection must do what is necessary to make sure that this will be done. Then secondly, to prevent possible looting, he can also order the military police attached to the brigade. He could order the military police to check the behaviour of the soldiers to make sure that they do not carry out any looting of civilian property. So he's giving orders. And then thirdly, he knows that because in this operation there will be casualties, so he needs the help of the medical department. He needs nurses, he needs doctors, and so on. So he will tell his assistant in charge of the medical department, Find me two doctors and four nurses. Then he also needs a logistical support. The operation might continue for a number of days, and there's need for food supplies. So he will ask the assistant in charge of logistics to prepare for the food supplies. Then when he gave all these orders, he can launch the operation, but in your -- in the system -- in your system, at least as I understand it -- let me finish first. Let's say that this operation is extremely well-prepared. So he's also going to ask the IPD to carry out some disinformation among the local population, sending pamphlets and so on. So also needs the help of the IPD. But in the system that you describe, it seems that the IPD, who is in the parallel chain, will go up to the Ministry of Defence to say, The commander of the brigade told me to do this or that. Do you agree with that? The assistant in charge of the medical department will also go all the way back up to the Ministry of Defence to say, I've been asked for four doctors and two -- two doctors and four nurses. Do you agree? Yes or no? And then what can the brigade commander do? Absolutely nothing. So tell me how can all this work? How can this function?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the first part, Judge Antonetti, I do agree with that. You stated that very correctly, but perhaps not the second part. They were prepared, according to that line of theirs, to give the commander what he needed. So you would sit down to a table. You would plan an operation, and you would calculate in the number of wounded, and then the assistant Medical Corps officer would say this will be the first place for pulling out the troops. Here we'll do the selection, deciding who was going to be taken to hospital first, and for that number, they would see what the roads were like, what routes could be taken. They would look at the house where the people would be taken to first. And perhaps he might need one or two cars that he didn't have at the time. Then he has this line of his, and he's -- so this is no longer the job of the commander. It's his job down the vertical chain. He can say, All right. We're planning this in Rama. And he's going to bring in two cars, having received permission from Tomislavgrad or from wherever else. So just like in a modern society, the fire brigade, the firefighters are prepared for any eventuality. They have their structure, they have their commanders, they have their men, but when a fire breaks out, you, as the mayor, ring up the fire brigade and then they do their job, or you ring up the police, and the police does its job. And it's the same structure mirrored in society or the IPD. So I created the structure. I set up the IPD structure to be in the service of the commander, and then the IPD man would say, This unit that you prepared to take action along this axis according to information supplied by my psychologist had too many dead and wounded last time, so to the best of our knowledge it isn't enough -- you don't have enough men to fulfil the task, perhaps you could use another battalion from the brigade and deploy them. So there we have the structures with their organisation, and, to be quite frank, that's what I did, same as logistics. The logistics man would say, I need so much of such a thing and so on, and then the other person would say, We don't have that many shells. We don't have that many bullets. We don't have two BKs combat sets but just one and a half, or whatever, and the commander will decide whether, despite all this, he will go into action or not. So he'll weigh everything up, weigh all the information up, and then decide what he's going to do. Seeing the number of -- the amount of ammunition he has at his disposal, he will look and see whether there are enough vehicles to pull out the wounded, whether his units are ready for combat, and the psychologist will help him there, psychologist from the IPD. Unfortunately, we didn't have them in the HZ apart from the knowledge that he already has. And when he puts this whole picture together he's going to say, Right, we move tomorrow at 6.00 a.m.; or, No, we don't move tomorrow. We're going to wait for two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My observation is page 33, line 13, where the translation is giving, "Just like in a modern society." And I think what was meant was a modern corporation, or something like that, a modern business. With you agree, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be quite frank, in societies or companies that's how it's organised, as far as I know. And I think I do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have something to say with respect to the transcript before it's lost -- well, it's lost now. In line 32 -- page 32, line 24, Mr. Praljak said you're quite right with respect to this first part, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, and with respect to the second part, you said, Mr. Praljak, he should not have come. So did you mean you -- you said he didn't have to ask, he was already preparing or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he had at his disposal what he was preparing to have, that's all right. But if he was lacking two cars, he would go along his chain and ask them for two cars. It wasn't the brigade commander who could issue an order for those two cars to be sent. So if the IPD needed, say, five people from Zagreb for a specific operation, then he would ask the IPD man on the ground and say that it would be a good idea that in preparing the operation they should have more men, then the IPD would inform me, and I would send them. I mean we're complicating a very simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question from Judge Mindua. This is a very important topic, which is why we get so many topics from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely this topic is essential. Witness, I have a very short question. In this parallel system, as the President of the Trial Chamber said, let's say we have a commander that says he's going to launch an operation tomorrow morning at 6.00 a.m. The assistant then in charge of the medical department reports to -- what if he -- what if he tells the commander, No, this is ludicrous. You won't have any doctors. I can't give you any doctors. And the one in charge of the logistics says, I can't do anything, I don't want to do it, I want to go to the beach instead. So what can the commander do in this parallel system, you know, if everybody decides not to agree and not to go along with what the commander is asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander, at that very same moment, informs his superior officer, if it's a brigade, then the operation zone, the operation zone will inform the Main Staff, and I will inform Mr. Stojic, telling him that his services, the services within his scope, aren’t working properly and I want more men. So the commander can’t dismiss the man because he didn't appoint him. So no commander in the Croatian Army or the HVO can dismiss the IPD assistant whom I had appointed. However, through the chain, he can come to me and say, Look what's happened. Look what's happening to me. And then the man would leave straight away. He would be sent packing straight away. But that's not what happened. All he could say is, I don't have enough men for this operation, and I need another doctor, for example, and then he's going to go down his chain to ask for two more cars or bandages or whatever his service needs to place at his disposal, that's what it's for. But as far as I know, that's how armies function generally; otherwise, they just don't function. Well, Your Honour Judge Mindua, look at the American army, for instance, a commander or an operation can't issue orders to the air force directly, but he asks the chief of the air force to provide him with so many planes for a given operation, and so on and so forth. And even within the frameworks of the army, for example, the marines within the land army have their own headquarters and command, and it's not the land force commander of America that is in charge. He says, All right, we'll need marines for this operation. So these links and lines in the army is not as simple as one would wish, just one man, and then issuing orders to everyone. He does command an action, but support action, he needs support from meteorologists, the weather men, and so on, what the weather's going to be like, the tides when it comes to disembarking in Normandy, and so on and so forth. Hundreds of services are involved. When you throw flyers on German territory. It's not a service that Eisenhower was in charge of. He asked them to prepare things like that for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This answer doesn't satisfy me or not convince me, Mr. Praljak. The examples given by my colleague are examples, I would say, of gross refusal to obey an order. And I think a person like that ought immediately to be arrested and put into disciplinary arrest, because you cannot operate -- when you plan an operation as a commander for, let's say tomorrow morning 6.00, it would be something simple because it's a short time, you cannot first go up to complain with -- to the general -- to the chief of the General Staff who will then talk to the minister. How is that going to work in military situations, in a situation of war? I think that's absolutely absurd. I -- some commanders would shoot an assistant who, in this way, wants to sabotage an operation. I -- I don't think that can really work. How it's done then, that's the matter of the assistants, but when the commander decides there will be an operation, he may have discussed it before, is it possible, can it be done? But if he decides, he has the responsibility, and then everyone must go along. Otherwise, it won't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, while we're talking, this morning there's an all-out attack being launched -- just a minute. You're saying nothing. Does this mean that you have nothing to comment regarding the question my fellow Judge told me -- you? Do you have any answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you started speaking straight away, but I was waiting to see what you were going to say. Now, Judge Trechsel, first of all we were talking about preparations for action, and they refused and so on. It never happened. Well, what you were talking about never actually happened, well, to arrest. I don't know. Everybody would react. I would, of course, have beaten him, to be quite frank, but it couldn't have happened in the first place. What should I tell you? What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In armies, 99 per cent of things that happen in an organised army has -- all the problems have been solved hundreds of years ago or dozens of years ago. You can't have soldiers saying, I don't want to take part in an action, if the action is just about to begin or is under way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The -- we are in agreement for once. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as I was telling you, just as we're talking, today there's a major US offensive in Afghanistan with more than 4.000 marines sent in the framework of an all-out attack. And in this kind of operation, of course logistics, as well as the IPD and their medical department is managed by the commander in charge of the operation. It's difficult to imagine that in such an operation the medical department will be calling Washington to say, The commander wants to do this. Can we go along with him? Yes or no? It's absolutely impossible to imagine this. The system that you're describing and we can understand seems to be totally impossible to implement militarily wise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, you are not right there on that score. He doesn't have to call Washington, because he's prepared everything beforehand, but, nonetheless, the logistics man prepared his part of the job. And if you read it carefully, you will see that logistics very often bought some bad flack jacks because someone stole some money for better ones or the helmets weren't of the proper quality or they didn't have the right kind of uniform for sand and sandy conditions, but anyway, the ammunition situation has been prepared. Everybody has prepared, whether well or not. But the commander then commands with what has been prepared, and when an action starts, for example, the offensive of Germans here at the beginning of World War I, for example, the commanders, Rommel, Manstein, Guderian. They went ahead with the first tanks. Now, in the rear behind them, you had their assistants who calculated and said, right, they passed -- they've traversed a 70-kilometre route today, so we have to send them that much food. The tanks have used up so much ammunition, so they need more. We need to send more fuel, and so on and so forth. So all this was prepared along different chains, and that was the case even then. Rommel did not report to his headquarters, the headquarters behind him in the rear for a month; whereas everything was functioning probably, because then, and later on, the whole action was prepared. Those who produce and manufacture know how much an army needs. They know how many planes the army is going to need. So he doesn't have to refer back to others if the action was well-prepared, if he was well-prepared. And that's what happens in armies, not only this army but in armies generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you answer by saying that each assistant prepares everything. So there is no need to refer to the Defence Department. It is important that you tell us this. It's time for the break now. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, it seems to me that His Honour Judge Antonetti has somewhat simplified, thereby mistakenly summed up your answer. So in order to avoid any -- anything remaining unclear, I should like to ask you to try and to sum things up together. If I understood your statement correctly, what you said was that in the case of the preparation of simpler military operations where nothing major or significantly different is expected, the Medical Corps of the brigade will be prepared to offer health support to such an action, and that, therefore, it will not have to address, according to its line of specialisation, to these -- it will not have to address the sector of health of the Ministry of Health -- of Defence. But if a major operation is in question, if heavy casualties and wounded are expected for which the Medical Corps of the brigade is not prepared and that the expect -- it is expected that a larger number of vehicles will be required, a larger number of surgical teams, for instance, in that case, for such needs, the assistant commander of the brigade for the Medical Corps will address Dr. Bagaric, as man number one of the war health department, and he shall ask for assistance in preparing in major operation. Is that the gist of your response?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I don't agree with what Mrs. Alaburic has just said when she said that I had erroneously summed up your answer. If I had erroneously summed of your answer, you would have reacted straight away. When I said that in this dual chain which existed at the time, which you -- in which you told us that the brigade commander, after having heard various people, you told us that it was -- it wasn't necessary for the assistants to refer to the Defence Department if they were able to meet the needs put forward by the brigade commander. That is your position, isn't it? If that's not your position, please let me know. I had rather you tell me than your counsel, than Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not think that you misinterpreted me, but probably Mrs. Alaburic did. It is very simple, in fact. The brigade commander actually makes an estimation of the possible casualties, of the dead and wounded, and then his assistant says to him, Okay. I have sufficiently organised things. As far as I'm concerned, you can proceed with the action; or he can tell me, I want a 24-hour delay because I need more people, more vehicles, more bandages, et cetera; or, I have to see whether they have two surgical teams in the third echelon, because if you're expecting to have 40 wounded men, then what I know exists there will not suffice. So it is a simple matter, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just fill in a step, which I think got perhaps lost. There is to contradiction of what -- what Mr. Praljak has said and what Mrs. Alaburic has said, but the example of Ms. Alaburic refers to the level of the operation zone. If it is on the brigade level, then the medical chief of service at the brigade will first address the operational zone to see whether they can assist him, and only if that does not work then the chief on the operational zone level will go to the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. That depends on the level of the operation. If the operational zone can provide it all then he doesn't go any further. Why should he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you. And we have not forgotten what you have told us about jumping the line of command sometimes, because that may happen, but in principle, I think this is quite clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, we endeavour to be very precise and very fair. In connection with His Honour Judge Trechsel's question, the commander of the operation zone would not apply to the minister but to the assistant minister for health; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Why should he do that job with the minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually, I may have misspoken. Not the commander would contact him but that the chief -- the assistant of the commander would contact his superior, the assistants of the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, it was just as Judge Trechsel said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as the minister of defence is concerned, it is of no -- it doesn't make any difference whether someone would address Bagaric or you as the commander of the HVO, because the minister of defence is the superior of both Bagaric and you, yourself, as far as health is concerned; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bagaric, he's Bagaric's superior that's for sure, but the minister of defence is not superior to me in operational tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, that is why I'm asking you about the subject of health. I'm not asking you about the commanding of military operations. What I'm asking you about is everything that concerns the topic of health.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correctly -- correct as far -- it is the minister who manages all health affairs through his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to waste my time on this topic. Let's go to the next document, which is 4D1464. We're still in the first binder. That is the annual plan of work of the Ministry of Defence for the year 1994, but we shall look at it in order to see whether certain services also dealt with the same things during your period. The Croatian text, the e-court page is 4D270553. So it is 4D270553. And in the English text 566. These are only the last figures. That, for you, General, is page 3 of this document. It is stated that the task of the security sector is to supervise and control the work of administration centres and assistant commanders of SIS in HVO units and to undertake measures to promote their work. It emanates from this provision that the sector of security of the Department of Defence - and I correct myself - of the Ministry of Defence, supervises the work of the assistant commanders of SIS in the HVO units. Is that precisely this vertical line that leads to the sector of security from the individual HVO units where SIS issues are concerned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next page, the political activities sector. In the English text, it is e-court page -- just the last numbers, 569, and in the Croatian text it is 554. General, for you it is the end of page 4. It says: "Sector for political activity": "Integrating all levels of the service for political activity into a single system of subordination and coordination of the political administration of the Ministry of Defence of the HR HB, and developing an operative system for relaying information from the administration to individuals in the unit." Is this that vertical chain of communication, vertical line of communication concerning the IPD duties that we have been discussing so far, General? Was it like that in your time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be like that. It should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please now go to chapter 7, the "Main Staff." It stems from this document. The page in English is 576 and 558 in Croatian. It is your page 8, General. It stems from this document thus, that the Main Staff is part of the Ministry of Defence, and the Ministry of Defence adopts plans of work for the Main Staff as well. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We do not have the time to read this passage, but you have seen the document, I expect. There is no -- not a single reference in this document to the effect that the Main Staff would perform any duties from the ambit of the SIS, of the military police, of the health sector, the military judiciary, or the -- or criminal prosecution. Tell me, during your time, these were not duties within the competence of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were not duties within the ambit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the next document which, Your Honours, is in the small binder. It is P4699, a work report, for the first half of 1993. It is not your period, but let's look at what service did what. Of course we shall also deal with the Defence Department. General, look at page 4 of your document. In e-court, English text E-773. It states that the report of the Main Staff of the HVO is not a component part of this report because of secrecy and can be read in the office of the president of the HVO. This is something that we dealt with during the Defence case of Jadranko Prlic, but let us focus on what we are interest in. On page 18, General, we are dealing with SIS, S-I-S. In the English text, this is the ERN which ends in 781. The SIS administration on page 18, third paragraph. I quote: "The service has registered a series of crimes, of thefts, smuggling, armed robberies, murders, rapes, stealing of motor vehicles and other committed by the members of the HVO, both military persons as well as civilians, both in the area of Central Bosnia as well as in Mostar and other municipalities." What I've said now, General Praljak, is consistent with what you have been telling us to the effect that the SIS was involved in the detection of the perpetrators of criminal offences and the undertaking of measures to put the perpetrators of crimes on trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the fundamental duties of the SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
