utterances.text: The next part of the report has to do with the military police on which I do not wish to dwell on this occasion, but I just wish to draw attention to the fact that it is recorded that there is a sector for crime suppression -- a section for crime suppression and also information about the criminal complaints filed. Is that so, General, that this was a duty of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the duties of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at the moral development sector. That's page 18 of the English sector -- of the English text and page 27 of the Croatian text. It is stated here that still there are vacancies in brigades and in some military districts which are forcing -- according to establishment, have not been filled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the relevant page on e-court, please? It would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it is actually page 12, not 11, and 782, not 781 that you have quoted. You have summed this up by saying that SIS was involved. I quote from line 16, page 46, "In the detection and of the perpetrators of criminal offences." But what is stated here is only that they registered the crimes. That is no detection of the perpetrators. Where does it say that SIS detected perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the word "registered" is in quotation marks. If they know that those offences were committed by members of HVO, both civilians and military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I see it. It's very vague and general. It's not very specific. But then this is also a report, which, I think, one could expect to be much more specific, but it doesn't give any statistics, for instance, so-and-so many crimes registered, so-and-so many perpetrators identified, so-and-so many brought to justice, and so forth. It's just -- the informative content is light, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this report is what it is. The reports are usually very short because the service is a secret service. I can't add anything to the reports. I'm only interested in the report as such, and I wanted us to see what service was doing what, and that was my only objective at this moment. Let's go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I understood that, and I would not be understood as inviting you to add to the report or take away in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that for a moment I felt guilty for not having been able to provide you with a more detail -- a more detailed report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this report, it is stated that some places within the sector for morale in the brigades and other units are -- have not been filled up. Does this mean, General, that officials of the IPD and the brigades are part of the IPD service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at page 28, which is page 18 in English, if my notes are correct. At the very bottom of that page, General, it is stated that the sector for IPD, active participation in a meeting with IPD personnel in the army district of North-West Herzegovina, which was held in Rama on 17th June, and which assessed the degree of combat morale and priority tasks of the IPD in individual units. Tell me, please, does this correspond to -- I shall repeat the end of my question. A meeting ... held on 17 June in Rama at which participants assessed the degree of combat morale and the priority task of the IPD in individual units." Does this correspond to what you knew and what you have told us about your work in Croatia to the effect that the sector of the Ministry of Defence for IPD prioritised the tasks of the IPD in units and coordinated their work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the principal tasks was the assessment of combat morale and taking measures aimed at boosting that morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's skip the rest of the report, and, for the first time in this courtroom, we're going to deal with something that the Ministry of the Interior was doing or, rather, the department for the interior. This is on page 33 of the Croatian version, and on page 21 of the English version. It is stated here about the police department: The police was dealing with the state of peace and order, and towards the end of the first paragraph they -- it is stated that they established that there was an increased rate of all sorts of criminal behaviour, theft, violence, and let me not go on reading any further. This whole chapter refers to the cases in which public law and order were violated and impaired, and on that occasion, I would like to ask you, General, is this what I was saying at the beginning of my cross-examination, and that was that other services were primarily dealing with the maintenance of public law and order, primarily the Ministry of the Interior within the scope of its limitations as they were at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task of the Ministry of the Interior. And only if the person involved was an armed person in military uniform, it was their duty to call the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now repeat or sum up. If we are to apply the model of defence of America, on the ground of America, then the example of the American occupation of Afghanistan and Iraq are not very good because the American authorities are far from the military command. And this would not illustrate well the problems that you encountered on the ground. This was the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the ground of Bosnia and Herzegovina; wasn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And to the extent possible, the services had to function.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the part of the report that speaks about the judiciary. This is on page 47 of the Croatian version, and the 30th page in the English version, wherein it is stated: "In the territory of Herceg-Bosnia, military district courts were established as well as the military district prosecutor's offices. The connection of these bodies with the justice department is evident through the professional supervision and decisions, and they are in financial and organisational terms with the Defence Department. The connection of these bodies with the justice department is evident through the professional supervision and decision on appeals against military court rulings handled by the higher courts, that duality is used here where it says that this duality will most probably be removed by the new courts of law act. I know that you have not been dealing with the issue of military -- of the military judiciary but does this reflect your knowledge about the functioning of the military judiciary system?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this does reflect what I knew, but for the sake of the truth, we have to say two things here: The first thing, something that I'm very familiar with, is the fact that the Ministry of Defence or, rather, the Defence Department was burdened with many more things that would have been more normal, the refugees, the order, everybody came to that ministry because they saw that as a way to deal with things, because other ministries were less efficient than the Ministry of Defence. When you are efficient, then it has its counter-effects. Second of all, Your Honours, in all these documents one thing has to be highlighted: There was no single structure within the HVO, starting with the Main Staff, the Ministry of Defence, the SIS, and so on and so forth that hides anything in their reports. These are not made-up data. We are talking about crimes, killing, very clearly. We are talking about theft, and we are describing the situation as it was. Ubi et orbi, representing to everybody including this Trial Chamber, and we say this is the way the cookie crumbles. Nothing can be hidden and nothing is hidden, indeed. I belive that this should have been said. It's very important to say that even when there's reference to the ethnical cleansing of Mostar, this goes beyond the scope of your topic, but it what to be said, it had to be highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, General Praljak. I'm going to try and prove this, that the Ministry of Defence was so heavily burdened with all sorts of things, without being properly equipped to carry out all of its duties, which left it unable to meet its duties properly given the objective circumstances that were against it. General, I'm now going to skip a few documents, and I'm now going to talk about criminal prosecution. I'm going to be talking about three documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before looking at other documents, my first question on this work report pertaining to the first six months of 1993. General Praljak, at the time had you been made aware of this report which was officially adopted on the 7th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't aware of that, but to be honest -- no, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report on page 16 in the English version, penultimate paragraph, the prisoners are mentioned. Since you said a while ago that nothing was hidden, I established a link with your sentence and what this paragraph states. On reading this paragraph, we can see that it says that there are 4.000 prisoners that have been taken prisoner, that several hundred are members of the Serb army, and that others are members of the ABiH. So we know that there are Serbian and ABiH prisoners. It also states that large number of prisoners are being given various tasks which leads to a number of escapes, and there is a complaint here. Perhaps there is an insufficient number of military policemen to deal with the problem. It says that prisoners are being questioned by SIS people as part of their investigations. The prison wardens are appointed and so on. So there is nothing more to say about this, but a conclusion, which a reasonable trier of fact could reach, is this: This report does state that the prisoners are the subject of investigations, and if investigations are conducted, theoretically speaking this comes under the responsibility of the Prosecutor or the investigating judge. Whether we're talking about civilian or military body, this would depend on each case. As the commander of the HVO, what is your position on this? Were some prisoners not the subject of investigations? What would be their status in instances like these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't answer your question. This had nothing to do with what I was doing. This had nothing whatsoever to do with what the battle-field looked like at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, let's talk about criminal prosecution. I believe that the Trial Chamber has not -- has not had enough explanation or proper explanation about this segment. You will find the documents in a special binder. The first one is P309. It's already an exhibit. This is a binding order issued -- or a mandatory directive by the head of the Defence Department on the application of current regulations and possible pronouncement of penal sanctions for acts committed against the armed forces of the HZ HB. This is a mandatory directive on the application of current regulations and possible pronouncement of penal sanctions for acts committed against the armed forces of the HZ HB. This mandatory directive is in keeping with the report on work and indicates that the military judiciary, in certain aspects, was connected with the Defence Department, and as a result of that, the head of the dense -- Defence Department issued this mandatory directive. Tell me, were you familiar with this mandatory directive which was published in the "Official Gazette" of Herceg-Bosna in September 1992, or did you not see it at the time because you were not there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this. I know that this was copied from the penal code. And if I remember it well, it was published for people to know. I don't know much about the judiciary, but I know that people had to be aware of possible punishment that might ensue from some actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. And now let's look at 4D1317. The Honourable Judge Antonetti also prepared the same document when he examined you, but he did not have the time to show it to you. So far we only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, I don't entitle you to say this. You are saying that I haven't had time to examine the document. What do you know about it? Why are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never said that. It would never occur it me to say that. I said that you did not put your questions about this document, but, rather, you put your questions about the criminal prosecution on the basis of Article 27, of the Decree on Military District Prosecutor's Office, and that's why we have still not been given the complete picture of -- of who was supposed to do what in terms of criminal prosecution in Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the Decree from the Law on Criminal Procedure, Article 148 thereof --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Praljak, do you have any explanation for the existence of this mandatory directive. It seems to take over articles from the military code. So does it have any proper normative value or is it just a recall? And if it's just a recall, how come it takes the form of a decree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it wasn't binding. Mr. Stojic was not the one who prescribed laws, but you will see later on from a document that Mrs. Alaburic incorporated among his documents. In Croatia, I wrote a lengthy letter that should have been distributed among the entire Croatian army, simply to demonstrate to people what punishment ensued from what acts. And I believe that Mr. Stojic's intention was the same, to tell people what awaits them, and you will see this later if Mrs. Alaburic shows how I did it in Croatia. We had to show people how much sentence they will be given if they commit a certain crime. This was just a -- tell people so that they can't say they didn't know. The state, albeit, being in a state of disarray, but things had to be done in the way they should have been done. He says under the law, for such violations or offences, you have to be punished. I don't see any other sense to this mandatory directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do you believe that this recall was useful? We know that when you -- you already told us that going to gaol was seen as a rest more than anything. It was better to go to gaol than going to the front to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Mindua, a month or two in prison, yes; but ten years in prison for a heavy offence, ten years is not comparable with that for somebody who killed somebody or who inflicted an aggravated bodily harm. That's why people had to be aware of what awaited them if they offended. If one does something, one assumes that an instruction they issue, a seminar they organise, will bear results, and I claim that it, indeed, did bear results, but we will never know that for sure. History's just one and only. It is what it is. We cannot repeat it. We can only assume that certain actions bear results, and we proceed in that manner. I claim that results were visible, but things happened still, but that was simply part of that war, and it normally is part of any society, something that happens in every society, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you state that crimes were committed, but people were -- perpetrators were actually tried, convicted, sentenced for gaol sentences, long gaol sentences. Is that what you're stating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm that crimes were committed and that perpetrators were sentenced and convicted. That did happen. Anything else beyond that would be speculation on my part. There was a considerable number of those. Well, if you compare it to some other -- to what's happening in the suburbs of Rio de Janeiro, for example. I don't know whether that would be a large number then, but quite a few people were convicted of crimes, a large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, unless I'm very much mistaken, the Prlic Defence showed numerous documents about how people were prosecuted and convicted and sentences meted out, how the military courts worked, criminal reports filed, legal proceedings taken, and so on and so forth; you remember us discussing that in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and, Mrs. Alaburic, let me state again, I don't know anybody down it there from Utic [phoen] or Coric, or whoever, Stojic. I don't know a single one who did not do a lot of work and put in a lot of effort to improve the situation. I can't name a single person who did not do that or anybody who tried to hide anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more explanation, because it seemed to me that we had cleared this up during the last session, but then Judges -- Judge Mindua's question just now has shown me that we haven't clarified it fully. When you talked about prison, that you could -- that could be conceived as a rest or a reward, you spoke about disciplinary sanctions and prison in that regard, and a prison term of just a few days, not criminal proceedings, criminal action, and doing time on the basis of a criminal judgement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't have anything to do with the courts. I just said what the -- the kind of punishment that commanders could mete out and that was a maximum of 30 days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back now, General, to the document we were discussing. 4D1317 was the number, and you've told us everything already which I consider to be relevant, but we'll try and summarise that now. From Article 148 of the Law Governing Criminal Procedure, which was a Yugoslav war, which applied to -- and in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, to all state organs, and they were duty-bound to report crimes which are prosecuted ex officio. And along with the criminal report, they were also duty-bound to provide proof and evidence and to take steps to safeguard the traces of any crime that had been committed and objects with which or with the help of which a crime was committed and other evidence. So, General, that was an obligation on the part of all state and government organs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the citizens, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a little different where citizens were concerned, so let's leave that aside for the moment. Anyway, it was the responsibility of all state organs, including the Ministry of Defence, to act accordingly, to file a criminal report, to ensure that the evidence was kept safe and any objects involved, and so on and so forth, as is set out in this article, Article 148. Were you acquainted with that article governing criminal charges or crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, this obligation and duty in the Decree on Military Courts in Herceg-Bosna, in the district courts, was more fully elaborated for commanders of military units and military institutions. Now, General, you told us that according to your understanding, this provision related to situations when the perpetrator of a crime was known; is that right? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did understand me correctly, and this refers to when the perpetrator is apprehended, or to use your term, "in flagrante," red handed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a number of questions, along those lines to show Their Honours that what you say and claim is quite correct. And according to that provision, the commander of a military unit is duty-bound to take all necessary measures to -- to ensure that the perpetrator of a crime does not abscond or go into hiding.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For a commander to be able to take those steps, would the military commander have to know, first of all, who the perpetrator of a crime was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. He has to have him in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's right. He has to have him in his hands, because otherwise he cannot prevent him from going into hiding or escaping; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's move on. A military commander is also duty-bound to preserve the evidence and traces of a crime, which includes objects that can be used in evidence, as supporting evidence. Now, from that position, I would conclude logically that the traces of a crime and the objects involved must be in the location where the military commander is himself or somebody who can do that in his stead and in his name. Would that be logical?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If somebody from his unit apprehended the perpetrator of a crime, then they would have to secure that person, ensure that he does not abscond. And if it's a brigade, then they would send two or three military policemen or soldiers, if there were no military policemen available, to secure the site with all the objects used, if there was a rifle involved or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, generally speaking, let's look at the situation in Stupni Do. A crime had been committed. Eight days afterwards -- well, it wasn't eight. It was a little more, but for our working hypothesis, let's say ten days later, the area of Stupni Do came under the control of the BH Army, and the BH Army is in conflict with the HVO. Tell us now, please, in such a situation, the military commander of the HVO, can he fulfil his had duties and obligation of preserving the traces of a criminal act and the objects involved if they are still on the territory of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Alaburic, from what I have heard in this courtroom, the HVO, on the afternoon of the 23rd, left Stupni Do, and two days later, the Canadian Battalion and the investigative part of the Canadian Battalion took over all these acts, secured the site, counted the number of dead, and let's say there were a 150 of them there with all the journalists and everything else. As of that point in time, the HVO no longer had any control over that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you seem to have answered me -- answered my question in a roundabout way. Now, there's one more obligation that the commander is duty-bound to do and that is to collect all the information which could be of use to moving criminal proceedings, to initiate criminal proceedings. I think that this is self-evident, but if you need to add any comments please do so. You are nodding your head in the -- hand in the negative and saying you don't have any comments. So we can move on to another situation described in Article 151 of the Law Governing Criminal Procedure, and that's on the following page of this particular document, if we may turn to that now. And it shows the situation when there is reasonable doubt that a crime has been committed. And here we have enumerated seven basic duties that the organs of internal affairs or, rather, the police, have to fulfil. I'm going to enumerate them, and we'll comment. The first is to find the perpetrator of the crime.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, you said if the perpetrator of a criminal act was unknown, then some other provisions are applied and that work is done by the SIS and the police. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm staying with the same document. That's the document I refer -- I'm referring to. Let's go on with the duties and tasks. The second task and duty is that the perpetrator of a crime or accomplice should be prevented from escaping and going into hiding. So the organs of the interior have to take action there; is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Third duty is this: That all the traces of a crime be uncovered and preserved, as well as objects that may be used in evidence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the word "uncover," the word "uncover," is it logical to assume that we are dealing with investigation into the event to collect evidence for prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't think I need to explain in any greater detail this provision to the Judges. I think it's something that is common knowledge, because it's similar in every country, but let us just mention that you could gather information from citizens. You could conduct a search of flats, vehicles and all the other actions resorted to for the process of evidence collection. Now, let's see, General. Why did you say that this work, these -- this job, in military matters, should be perform by the SIS and the military police? In Article 25, on the provision governing district military courts, it says that the work and authorisation stipulated by the law on criminal proceedings, instead of the organs of the interior, are performed by authorised persons of the security organs of the armed forces. And the provision on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in Article 137, which is document P588, states that they are the security and information service. And in the last section, it goes on to say that the military police is authorised and has the obligation of taking action linked to crimes within the armed forces. Now, did you say that all that business, that is to say the investigation process, that that was up to the SIS and the military police; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I know how much more time I have, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, how much time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that an hour and 15 minutes, according to the calculations of my associate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, while we're waiting, General, let me say that I wanted to discuss the Main Staff with you, its establishment, services, and so on. So just briefly, let's go through some of these documents, and most of them are exhibits already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar is telling me that so far you've used up 3 hours and 39 minutes, 3 hours and 40 minutes, to round it off. You had an extra 45 minutes, so theoretically, you still have an hour and six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I'll do my best to get through my examination quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's move on and let's look at the Main Staff, and the next document is from the second binder. It is P502. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I don't know that we've been getting interpretation in English for the last few sentences. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me repeat what I was saying. After quoting the number, P502, I said that it was a document about the provisional establishment of the Main Staff, which, in September 1992, was passed by the head of the Defence Department. And according to that document, the Main Staff was supposed to have 107 members. And with respect to the posts and functions that are elaborated in detail here, it appears that in the Main Staff, there was nobody who would be in charge of SIS affairs and military police affairs, and health, and at the IPD. Is that really how it was, General Praljak

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Half of the Main Staff was not filled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We shall come to at that eventually. I should now like to talk about the SIS. If I understood your questions correctly, in the cross-examination of Mr. Ivan Bandic, who was a Defence witness for Bruno Stojic, you actually disputed the contention of the Defence of Bruno Stojic to the effect that in the first half of -- in the second half of 1993, when you were there, there was an official in charge of SIS in the Main Staff. Did I understand your question correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't know of the existence of that person. That is one thing. And secondly, I had never agreed to any appointment of his. Thirdly, I was not informed of his appointment. Fourthly, Mr. Bandic, to my question whether he had ever had a meeting with me and my assistants, he replied that he had not. So my question whether he had sent me any reports at any time, he replied that he had not. And actually, I only saw him when he was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I don't know what you mean "leaving."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you mean when you were leaving.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you told that Ivica Lucic was the first man of the SIS of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Ivica Lucic wrote articles about the security and intelligence services of both the former Yugoslavia, Croatia, and Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, his Ph.D. thesis was on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at 4D1311. Tell me, have you ever read this article by Mr. Ivica Lucic before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to just one segment, which I'm interested in at this point, and that is on page 9 of the Croatian text and on page 2 of the English text. So man number one in SIS says that there were no SIS service officials at all in the Main Staff of the HVO. Namely, he's claiming the same thing that you claim, General Praljak. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. There were no SIS officials there at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let us now -- no. Let me ask you one thing first. Something remains unclear. When colleague Nozica was showing you the documents signed by Mr. Ciro Grubisic, this is document 2D338, and Ciro Grubisic signed that document as head of the political administration of the Main Staff, I think. And you said that you didn't know that he had ever been appointed to the Main Staff. Am I interpreting your words properly, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't -- I have no idea. I don't know that he ever did anything in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was there any political administration in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it possible for this situation to have been that Mr. Tole, the Chief of the Main Staff, had actually brought Mr. Grubisic and that he worked there for a few days without ever having been appointed to the post which he signed and his signatures; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such a situation could have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the actual structure of the Main Staff. General Praljak, it is my intention for us to show Their Honours, especially His Honour Judge Antonetti, how it was that the Main Staff, in fact, functioned, because I have understood from the numerous questions posed by His Honour Judge Antonetti that he believes the Main Staff of the HVO to have been a group of top educated and schooled generals and other officials who were receiving numerous reports from the ground analysing the situation, pouring over maps, and on the basis of their analyses of the situation adopted decisions as to their further course of action. Such a perception of the Main Staff is logical, and I personally have the same perception of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think that this was the way His Honour Judge Antonetti perceives the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I shall be asking you questions, which I believe to be relevant, on the basis of what are my conclusions is desirable for Their Honours to know, but let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again, I'm sorry to rise. But it's very transparent from the face of the question that once again my learned friend is interposing her own views as to the nature of the case. I think cross-examination, it's not that difficult. The question can simply be posed. The conclusions, of course, are for Your Honours to draw, but what counsel may or may not think is clear or is not clear is really hardly the point. I would simply encourage my learned friend, with the greatest of respect, to simply phrase the questions and put those questions to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, put your question and refrain from providing us with your own interpretation. And whether the answer provided by the witness suits you or doesn't, then you can ask an additional question, if you wish. I have understood that what you wanted to highlight was the issue of the Main Staff, whether they were competent or not, and then address the question without providing us with your own view on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for your instructions. I should just like to say to my learn colleague Mr. Khan that there is no need to defend His Honour Judge Antonetti from me, and my comment had not so much to do with the essence of the question, which I am to put, but with the reasons why I'm going to put those questions. My first question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. I do apologise. Your Honour, I wasn't raising -- I wouldn't ever be so presumptuous to think that any member of the Bench requires my inartful assistance or defence. I rose as a matter or form. It's the second time I have felt the need to rise today, and on both occasions, it has been focussed, in my respectful submission, on the same malady which is inflicting the questions put by my learned friend. It is the intermingling of questions which are proper and comment which is not. That's the reason I stood up. My learned friend put it very blatantly in her question what her view s are. The views of counsel are irrelevant. Not only that, they are inadmissible, and that is the reason I stood up, not to defend the honour or to defend any member of the Bench. Far be it from me to presume such a role. I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, put your questions and remain from making any personal comments and then things will run smoothly. Mr. Khan is quite right, and I would like to thank him. I don't need counsel to defend me, and I don't need to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Praljak would like to leave the courtroom for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I seize this opportunity to reply. I do not believe Mr. Khan is right. I apologise for misinterpreting his intervention, and I must admit that I did not understand as actually coaching me in the sense of what questions should be posed during the cross-examination. If Mr. Khan wanted to teach me a lesson about the kind of question I should put, I thank him very much. I believe that that is not necessary. And if he had any different objections to my question, he could have raised that as a substantive objection to my question. So I did not advance any theses of mine. I just simply wanted to say why in continuing I shall be dealing with so prosaic, apparently prosaic a question as is the number of people who worked in the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, technically speaking, you wanted to highlight the fact that according to you and according to Mr. Petkovic, since you should provide us with his point of view, that the Main Staff was not exceedingly competent. Before reaching this conclusion, you put a question to Mr. Praljak, and you asked him to describe to us about how the Main Staff operated, and he will say, There were a few officers, and you add, These officers were trained or were they not trained? And he will say, No they were not good. And then you say, Can one, therefore, conclude that the Main Staff was not extremely competent, and he can say, Yes, I can draw that conclusion. And that's it. You do it the other way round. You give the conclusion first and then you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was not at all my intention to dwell on competence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at document 2D1352, and let us look at the last page in this document. This is a payroll of the Main Staff for November 1992, and this list shows us that on this payroll there are 20 men; is that correct, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is it correct that Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic is not among the 20 but is indicated separately, although he is the head, because he received his salary from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, was this the period when the officials who have come from the Croatian army to assist the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina received their salaries in the same way? Who came as volunteers, whom you referred to before as coming to support both components in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell it us, General, according to the information that you have, is it true that in the Main Staff of the HVO, towards the end of 1992 there were between 20 and 25 people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the information that I have, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was anyone among them including Milivoj Petkovic -- did anyone among them have the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. We'll deal with that at the end. I wanted to talk about the conditions of work, but let us now look at the number a few months later. Take a look at the next document, P1683, namely. That is the manning of the Main Staff in March 1993. We have 33 persons there, and we also have two officers of the Croatian army working on a temporary basis in the Main Staff. So that would make a total of 35 men. Does that correspond to what you know about the number of people who worked in the Main Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us explain, General. When we say 20 -- 35 people, these include drivers, secretary, typist. All the auxiliary staff, in other words; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During that period, according to the signature, Mr. Petkovic was not yet a general.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else in this list have the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the document we have before us, 32 people are mentioned. That is right. Turn the page, please. I believe I've put the question already. This this goes back a few months, perhaps even a few years. We can see that two officers from the Croatian army are mentioned, Miro Prce and Josip Speranza. What are these two officers doing there, those two officers from the Croatian army? Are they on an internship? Are they being trained? This part of military cooperation? What are they doing there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for Miro Prce to enlist, to report as a volunteer, to help Petkovic to actually deal with organisational establishment matters. So he simply came as a volunteer down there, just as I had taken those several volunteers to Central Bosnia to help us organise the establishment books, the brigades, et cetera, in the same way I asked him to go down there and he remained down there and became an HVO officers. As for this other person, frankly speaking, Speranza, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, a straightforward one. You have studied the foreign armies and each day you demonstrate that you are knowledgeable on these matters. The other armies, did they have the same amount of men, or did you have a very small number of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In foreign armies of such numbers there would be at least several hundred -- many in the Main Staff, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, the next document is P0 -- P907. This is a report for the year 1992, prepared by Milivoj Petkovic, and I should like us to focus on it in somewhat more detail. Let us look, first and foremost, what is said under bullet 3. It is stated there: "HVO forces organised themselves during combat operations throughout the area of the HZ HB." If I am not mistaken, this would corroborate your contention that there was no peacetime army that would shift to wartime conditions but that the army was, indeed, created in war conditions. Could we look at it that way, General, or can we interpret -- should we interpret it in a different way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army actually reared, created its own self. It was not created by somebody else. It was created from within, on a voluntary basis, and in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. A preliminary technical question. This report purports to cover the period from 14 April 1992, to 31st December 1992, but it seems to be dated from the 15th December. Is this a matter of prophecy, part of it, or how -- how is this to be understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask you to look at the Croatian text, and you will see that the dates were corrected by hand. This is a Prosecutor's document, and the translation is very correct, very good. You will see that the last date of that period is 15 December. And this was crossed out and somebody added, in their own handwriting, 31st December 1992. You will find this also in the English translation of this text. Therefore, the author did report up to the 15th of December, but the subsequent handwritten intervention applies to the entire year 1992, but I don't think that -- this goes against the gist of the document, which, for that matter, is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The enigma is not solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I would like to tell you whose handwriting this is and whose intervention this is, but I don't know it. This is a Prosecutor's document. Maybe my learned friends from the Prosecution may shed some light or maybe General Praljak has the answer. Could this be deducted from the Chamber's time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever intervened, whoever corrected, did not do much harm. Nothing changed within the 15 days, as far as the report goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let's continue dealing with bullet 3 which speaks about the manning, and it says that in the Main Staff the strength is 30 per cent, that the command of the South-East Herzegovina OZ is 95 per cent strength, that the two operative zones are up to 60 per cent of their strength, whereas the OZ Posavina, is up to 40 per cent of its strength. As far as you know, General Praljak, throughout the war in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, was the situation more or less the same, which means that the commands of the operation zone and the commands of the brigades were much more -- much better manned than the Main Staff itself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, Mrs. Alaburic, this status of replenishment is based on the establishment which is very, very, austere and compared to any modern army, it is already two times less than it should be in comparison with the number of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we will come to the part of the document that speaks about that. Can you now look at page 3. There's a list of brigades, which were established toward the end of 1992, and after that, there is a summary which says the total number of men in all the HVO units is 45.000, and in the professional army units, there are a total of 855 men. My question to you, General, is this: Wouldn't that be exactly what you answered in -- to Judge Antonetti's question when he asked you how many men you had and how much of that were professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This corresponds to what I remember about the situation -- or, rather, about what I knew about the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at bullet point 4 in the same document where it is stated that there were problems with planning and mobilisation, and it is stated that in the territory of HZ HB, there is a very few Croat officers and non-commissioned officers from the former army: "The number of trained reserve officers and NCOs is also unsatisfactory. The defence of this territory and the command of units, in most cases, rests on 'ordinary men' who have no military knowledge but are devoted to the ideas of the HZ HB officers of the Croatian army have given great help." General wouldn't that be a summary of what you had tried to tell us about the -- the education and training of the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As far as the great help on the part of the HV army, it was not that great. There was some help and we appreciated it, but it was not at that great.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the conclusion, because I believe that this conclusion is very significant in light of the intentions of the HVO. It says here: "The HVO forces, despite many problems and difficulties, are managing to hold under their control 70 per cent of the free territory in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It seems that I have misspoken. It says, "the free area in Bosnia and Herzegovina." It stems from this sentence -- or, rather, what could we conclude, based on this sentence, as to what the HVO is defending?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the 70 per cent of the free territory, what territory is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territory that was not occupied by the Republika Srpska army. At that time, we held 70 per cent of the non-occupied territory. We managed to defend it, and BiH army managed to defend the remaining 30 per cent of that territory, and later on we were chased out of the territory in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say you were chased out, who do you mean? Who chased you out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's look at the following sentence. Milivoj Petkovic says: "By having created its armed forces in the territories of the HZ HB, the Croatian people managed to defend itself and large -- largest part of Muslims." Could you please provide your own comment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Go on then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO put up resistance against Republika Srpska and at that time, there were no nationalist thoughts. Croats defended both themselves and Muslims in an equal way. Their permanent desire was a desire for cooperation, and we've said everything else. There's nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. I'm now going to skip a few documents. However, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm going to try and solve the mystery over the date. Look at the document in B/C/S. The document has seemingly been signed by Mr. Petkovic. Initially, this document bore a number. As you can see, a new number was put on the document since two extra paragraphs were added on, five and six, which means that the document now contains seven paragraphs. We have a feeling that there was an initial text. Somebody reviewed the document and modified the document in question. I'll get back to this later. Perhaps Mr. Petkovic signed it, and then he realised that it wasn't right, and he made corrections, which is possible, or somebody else modified the text. Now, what is more interesting is the corrections made. This text was send to the head of the Defence Department and then it was crossed out. Immediately above, you have two asterisks with mention two things. Seemingly, it stated training of new recruits and personnel. Do these two asterisks coincide with the paragraphs 5 and 6 that are empty? I don't know. But even better, the text has been corrected and two things have been crossed out. I'd like to mention to you what has been crossed out. A, "helped by the forces of the Croatian army." This has been crossed out. And further down it says, "Forces of the HVO and a battalion from the Croatian army." What has been crossed out is, "And a battalion from the Croatian army." Can you see this? Is it possible that the person who signed the document read it over again and crossed this out or was this done in a different manner? This is a technical question I have for you. The mere fact that there is a correction here would explain why the date is the 31st of December, 1992, after the document has been corrected. The person, therefore, feels that the document would then include the two extra paragraphs. This is just an assumption I'm making, which is what it's worth. This is why, perhaps, the state figure is on the document, the 31st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Petkovic is there. He will answer these questions. The only thing I have to say is this: There is no dispute that a battalion of the Croatian army that I already mentioned, about 159 or 160 men strong, participated in April 1992 to fill up a gap in the line through which the Yugoslav People's Army could pass. There's no dispute about the fact that those people assisted in the liberation of the right bank of the Neretva River, and I believe that, at the time in question, they were no longer there. I believe that sometime in early summer or late summer, they left. And the second sentence that has been crossed out. I'd like to say that there's no dispute about the fact that the HVO, as it was liberating the southern part of Croatia, also assisted with the liberation of Stolac. I'm talking about the part that from Metkovic. There's no dispute about anything here. However, Mr. Petkovic will be much better suited to answer your questions because this is his document, but the things that I've just told you now are the things that I'm aware of, and I've already spoken about those things in very precise terms. I spoke about the role, the time, the place, everything in very precise terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, which is much more important than what is been deleted or issues relating to a date. This particular document states that there were 45.000 men in the units of the HVO. You have told us, and we've seen the documents pertaining to that, that the HVO, the way it was set up, may not have been ideal, given that some men had deserted and that there was a lack of military spirit within these units. However, it states that 857 members are part of the professional units of the army, 85 officers and so on. Technically speaking, it seems that the HVO had a professional army amounting to a thousand people maximum, and the other men are people who had been drafted. Was the HVO not, true to fact, an army which comprised a thousand very well-trained professional soldiers and the other men were, perhaps, people that were not so well-trained? What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 855 men were separate. They were the best from the existing units. They were separated from the units, and they were not in the same place. They were subdivided into five or six groups of which one was in Bosnia, one in Livno, one in Capljina. They were extracted from the troops. I'm talking about the Bruno Busic Unit. I would say that in any one place they had about 80 to a hundred men. Even at that unit was not complete. It was broken up across the territory. But they were at one's disposal around the clock. Once they completed their task or a mission, they did not go home. They were at one's disposal around the clock. If they were not engaged, then they were billeted in a military facility. And you could mobilise them, and immediately they could react. This saved you sending call-up papers, gathering men who would take time to be mobilised. It was a unit, and there were too few of them anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for a break. We'll have a 20-minute break, and then we'll have an hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I think I understood that Mr. Kovacic wanted to take the floor at the very end of the session. How long will you need, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Although I did ask to be allowed time at the end of the day, but I can do it now. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that General Praljak's Defence, before the cross-examination, informed the Trial Chamber that we had voluntarily given up on our contacts with the accused in order to contribute to the credibility of his testimony. However, we wish to pay a visit to the accused very briefly, but we will still adhere by the restriction imposed upon us. We would like to talk to him about the technical preparations of our case once he finishes his testimony. I'm talking about some technical issues and calendar issues, because as you know, in two weeks we go on recess, and we have to submit some information to the other parts -- parties in the proceedings and the Trial Chamber before the 1st of August, which imposes some limitations on us, and we have to agree on some things. I would like to inform everybody that we will be talking to our client tomorrow, but our conversation will not deal with any issues pertaining to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you know that the Trial Chamber has issued decisions on this matter. During this phase the Trial Chamber allows for contacts between the accused and his counsel; but the Trial Chamber reminds the counsel that there is a code of ethics and that he's not supposed to pressure his client into testifying in a certain fashion. You know all this anyway. And you're telling us anyway that you will only mention calendar issues. Very well. You kept us abreast of what you were going to do. Thank you. You didn't have to do this, so thank you for volunteering this information. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, let me just tell you how we're going to proceed for the next 45 or 50 minutes that I still have left. I would like to finish with the Main Staff and the disciplinary procedures, and then I would like to move on to some documents that pertain to you directly, and then depending on the time I have left after that, I would like to deal with some documents, which means that I will not have any more time to deal with any of the topics in a systematic way. In the set of documents that you have before you, can we look at document P293, which is the rule -- book of rules on military discipline. The document is already in evidence. General, could you please look at Article 67 thereof. In article speaks about the persons who issued decisions on sending somebody to military disciplinary court. It's either the commander of the armed forces or the commander of the operations zone. I would kindly ask you and everybody else to retain this article in their memory, because I'm going to try and compare it with the book of rules on the military discipline of the Republic of Croatia. Could you please look at 4D1346 now, 1346, which is the book of rules on disciplinary -- military discipline of the Republic of Croatia, and could you please look at Article 69 thereof. If we compare the two rules of military discipline. We will see that they are almost identical. The wording of the rules is almost identical; isn't that the case General? Could you establish that while you were reading it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, with the caveat, that there's no air force and navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at Article 69, according to which in the Republic of Croatia the decision to bring the offender before the military disciplinary court shall be issued by, under one, the Chief of the Main Staff, and, under 2, the commander of the operative zone. If we go back to the previous Article 67 in the Herceg-Bosnian document, we will encounter the following situation: What in Croatia is the Chief of the Main Staff and what he could do there. I'm talking about Article 67 in the regulation on the military discipline of Herceg-Bosnia. And I shall repeat the entire sentence, because I cannot do it by simply correcting the transcript. If we compare Article 69 in the Croatian regulation, I have to word my question. If we compare Article 69 in the Croatian regulation with Article 67 in the regulation of Herceg-Bosnia, it seems that what the Chief of the Main Staff could do in the Croatian army -- the transcript is frozen on our screen. Now we have it. Very well. So what the Chief of the Main Staff could do in the Croatian army is not what the Chief of Staff could do in the HVO. Tell me, general, as you compared these two regulations, is one all right to reach such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the HVO, it was the commander of the armed forces who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now go on to 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a small question. I may be completely wrong. I seem to recall, Mr. Praljak, that you had said that you did not have time and the possibilities of setting up a disciplinary court in the HVO. Am I wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not me. That wasn't my duty. These courts, military disciplinary courts within the HVO were not established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I thought. So I find this a bit abstract as a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, my next question relates to military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General Praljak, look at document 4D1331, which is a decision by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, dated the 14th of November, 1991, on the establishment of military disciplinary courts in the Croatian army. Now, tell us, please, General, did you know that in the Croatian army military disciplinary courts were established and functioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General Praljak, in Herceg-Bosna, the President Mate Boban, did he ever make a similar decision on the establishment of military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that completes that topic. I'm going to move on to another area now, General. Documents from the last part of binder 3, and the title of that section is "Other Documents." The first of these is a document numbered 3D3316. It's an information about the frequency of crimes committed by members of the Croatian army, which you, General Praljak, as assistant to the Croatian minister of defence, passed on the 1st of October, 1992. Tell us, please, General, is this a document that you referred to several times during the examination-in-chief and a moment ago when you mentioned prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, did you mean P01336?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The number is correct. It's all fine. But I'm now going to deal with the documents in binder 3, in the last section, the last section of binder 3, at the very end of the third binder. So the first document in that last section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, your B/H/S is improving from one day to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You mean from one year to the next, Madam Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're going to be around together for at least another year, I think we'll all be speaking the language.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, I read this information of yours, but I'd like to hear from you. As the assistant defence minister, what to your mind was the most important thing in this report, but please be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple. This was sent out to all the operative zones, and the IPD services, to the Croatian navy, and air force defence, right down to the IPDs in the companies. It's a long text, but anyway, what was happening with crimes? Crimes were being committed. And one of my duties was to -- for this information to reach each and every soldier, to tell them what it's about. So in a way this is my ID card, my personal ID card, and I state, under number 1 that the Croatian army was victorious in the war, and that for the first time, the possibility of -- was able to set up its own democratic state. And I quote: The first and basic condition for the existence and activities of a country like that is the rule of law, is that there be the rule of law, and because of that, nobody, not even the present or previous HVO [as interpreted] members, can go unpunished if they violate the country's laws and regulations. In point 2, I go on to say that regardless of all the merits that someone might have and the personal sacrifices they might have made, nobody, and I quote, nobody gained the right and privilege to avoid punishment for a crime or for that punishment and sentence to be mitigated and, let alone, be forgotten altogether. And then I go on to explain in great detail the length and breadth of it all, the laws. You see, Judge Trechsel, I did deal with laws. And I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think there's a correction or clarification in the transcript that needs to be made. On line 13, it says HVO, and I think since we're referring to a Croatian army document, it's probably is meant to be HV.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. I just have one additional question. In line 6, on that same page, it was recorded that you said that -- you say my duties. When you say "my duties," you mean your duties as assistant defence minister for IPD; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You must understand one thing, and it is this: We have a list of the number of suicides, for example, committed, people shot in -- in certain situations, some people committed crimes others killed themselves, and there were very many suicides just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is an interesting document. There are a number of things, but legally it seems that it raises a problem. You're talking about the situation of soldiers of the Croatian army who were demobilised and then committed crimes, but if they've been demobilised then they've become civilians; and if they're civilians, this must come under the jurisdiction of civilian courts. So what did you mean exactly there, demobilised but they're still soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. This has to do with soldiers, but if they commit a crime while in the army, then they are -- that crime and an investigation and so on will catch them up even when they cease to be Croatian army soldiers. The fact that they were brave soldiers, brave Croatian soldiers, will not be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction to the transcript once again and we can have Mr. Praljak's explanation. Page 86, line 10. General Praljak said that in certain situations, some people committed -- it's one line down. We had numerous suicides, for example, people shot in certain situations. It says people shoot in -- shot in. To -- this was the -- it's the same -- they -- it's the same word. When the word "pucati" is used, what does General Praljak mean in shoot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the decompensation of that person. They lost it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In colloquial terms, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak let's look at the next document, 3D3260. It's a letter which Franjo Tudjman in January 1991 sent to the American President George Bush.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: George Bush, Sr.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, senior. And in my opinion what is important here is what it says in the fourth paragraph about respect for internal borders and expectations of support from the United States of America. And we come back to the question of internal borders. When we speak about internal borders, we mean the borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This letter is one of a series of pieces of evidence from Dr. Franjo Tudjman in an attempt by writing this letter, once again, to explain what policies Croatia pursued and to indicate the capacity that could befall the country if, and he's asking the president of the United States to send a message, a message from the USA could have prevented a catastrophe. Unfortunately, this letter just was not taken up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, this document was prepared by your Defence, so I assume that you are acquainted with its contents and already know about them. Now, let's look at the next document which is 3D272. 3D272. And this is important for understanding the intentions of Herceg-Bosna. It's a document from Mate Boban, from April 1992, and I'm going to give you a short summary of it because we don't have time to go into it in any great detail. In paragraph 4, Mate Boban says that there -- that there is a great war machine, a Serb army war machine that fell upon Croat and Muslim territories of Herceg-Bosna, and that was a quotation, on the Croatian and Muslim areas of Herceg-Bosna. And then he goes to enumerate the individual towns that were hit, that were attacked. And then further down he speaks of the destruction of Dubrovnik and Zadar and also mentions the destruction of the old oriental inner city in Sarajevo which was called Bascarsija. And it was further stated that this was one of the rare urban entities and architectural entities of Islamic art, examples of that in Europe. And then further down it goes on to speak of the dangers that this presents to the Croatian and Muslim people, and it goes on to say that the two ethnicities are dying out. And then he addresses the Croatian and Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he talks about that. Now, General Praljak, from all that, can we conclude that in April 1992, for the president of Herceg-Bosna, there was no dilemma, no doubt at all that the Muslims and Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina were, in fact, equally under threat from the Army of Republika Srpska and that their interests, with respect to the Army of Republika Srpska and the aggression that they were exposed to, are indubitably common ones. Can you give us a different explanation, or how do you understand this document, this letter, particularly in light of the Prosecutor's case about the JCE?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how do you want me to explain it and interpret it? Not only that year but right up until an all-out open aggression by the BH Army, that is to say when killings started, when expulsion started, this was the policy and politics of the HZ HB and Mate Boban and all of us, in actual fact. There was joint criminal enterprise. Not only was there no joint criminal enterprise, but the situation was quite the reverse. It was all the way round.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, now let's look at the documents in the first binder, at the very beginning of the first binder. I think these documents in part relate to the Prosecutor's case about the joint criminal enterprise. The first document in this set is 4D1342, and it is a document about the parliamentary elections for the Republic of Croatia in 1990, and I just wanted to document for Their Honours this area. If we turn to page 3 of this document, and the number is 7, and the Judges could also take a look at the Croatian document, because not all the names have been translated. But anyway, here, General Praljak, we can see that on behalf of the Coalition of National Agreement, you were the counter-candidate in the same electoral unit to Franjo Tudjman, who was the HDZ candidate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, were those the elections that you mentioned earlier on as having been held in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now also us look at the next document. It is 4D1339. And this is a document about the programme and principles of the Coalition of National Agreement to which your party belonged, the HDS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, when asked by Judge Antonetti about the political programmes and political parties, you replied and said that the Coalition of National Agreement, and no other political party in Croatia in those 1990s, had in its programme any ideas about changing the borders of the republics.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in their wildest dreams.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, let's demonstrate that to Their Honours, and look at point 1. There Croatia is mentioned and its right to self-determination, its right to secession, and to joining up with other nations. Now, this right to self-determination, is that the right that you were asked about by the Judges pursuant to the Constitution of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that something that was guaranteed under the Constitution in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look for comparative purposes points 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, point 1, the last sentence there: "...this right shall be enjoyed by other republics as well as sovereign states."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, tell me, General, under the Yugoslav political system and Constitution of 1974, there was absolutely no doubt that the republics were states and that they were united into a common country which was Yugoslavia, and that was verified and set out in the Constitution in that way. Can you confirm that that was so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the right to self-determination, the way it was perceived from the angle Croatian political parties, it was always indubitably the right of the republics of the former Yugoslavia to exit Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indubitably so. In all the programmes of all the parties. I also participated in the drafting of this document and the source documents of the HDZ, the initial resolution of the HDZ, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
